# Facets and composition

There are two different reasons to end up with a grid of panels, and
vellumplot keeps them separate. *Faceting* takes one plot and splits it
by a variable, so every panel shares the same encodings and (by default)
the same scales. *Composition* takes several independent plots, each its
own spec, and arranges them into a single figure. Use faceting for small
multiples of the same view; use composition for a dashboard of different
views.

## Faceting

[`facet_wrap()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/facet_wrap.md)
lays panels out in a ribbon wrapped to `ncol` or `nrow`.

``` r

vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  facet_wrap(~cyl, ncol = 3)
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

[`facet_grid()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/facet_wrap.md)
puts panels on a 2-D grid defined by a `rows ~ cols` formula, which is
the right tool when you are crossing two variables.

``` r

vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  facet_grid(vs ~ am)
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Shared or free scales

By default position scales are shared across panels so the axes line up
and panels are comparable. When panels cover very different ranges, free
them per panel with `scales = "free_x"`, `"free_y"`, or `"free"`.

``` r

vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  facet_wrap(~cyl, scales = "free")
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

`scales = "free_y"` is sugar for the underlying
[`resolve_scale()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/resolve_scale.md)
lattice, which lets you set the policy per aesthetic directly. These two
are equivalent:

``` r

vplot(mtcars) |> mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  facet_wrap(~cyl, scales = "free_y")

vplot(mtcars) |> mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  facet_wrap(~cyl) |> resolve_scale(y = "independent")
```

### Long strip labels

Strip text is clipped to its strip, as in ggplot2, so a label wider than
its panel can’t run into the next panel or off the page:

``` r

regions <- data.frame(
  x = rep(1:4, 3),
  y = c(2, 3, 5, 4, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2, 1),
  region = rep(c(
    "Northern highlands and islands",
    "Central belt",
    "Southern uplands and the borders"
  ), each = 4)
)

p_long <- vplot(regions, width = 6, height = 2.4) |>
  mark_line(x = x, y = y) |>
  facet_wrap(~region, ncol = 3)
p_long
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

There are two ways out. `labeller = label_wrap_gen(width)` wraps each
label at `width` characters, and the strip grows to hold every line:

``` r

vplot(regions, width = 6, height = 2.4) |>
  mark_line(x = x, y = y) |>
  facet_wrap(~region, ncol = 3, labeller = label_wrap_gen(18))
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Or turn the clipping off with `theme(strip.clip = "off")` (ggplot2’s
values: the default `"inherit"` and `"on"` clip, `"off"` doesn’t), and
let a label that is only a little too long run past its strip.

### Independent colour, size and other legends

Colour, size and the other non-position scales are shared across panels
by default, so one legend describes the whole figure and a colour means
the same thing in every panel. When each panel has its own set of
categories, or values on very different ranges, a shared scale can waste
most of the palette.
[`resolve_scale()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/resolve_scale.md)
takes those aesthetics too: `"independent"` trains the scale in each
panel from that panel’s data alone, and each panel gets its own legend,
drawn beside its panel.

``` r

vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(gear)) |>
  facet_wrap(~cyl, labeller = label_both) |>
  resolve_scale(color = "independent")
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

`colour =` and `fill =` both name the colour scale; `size`, `alpha`,
`shape`, `linetype`, `linewidth` and `pattern` work the same way.
Independent and shared scales mix freely: here `hp` keeps one size
legend while each panel rescales its own colours.

``` r

vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = hp, size = qsec) |>
  facet_wrap(~am, labeller = label_both) |>
  resolve_scale(color = "independent")
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The per-panel legends sit right of each panel by default; each column of
panels gets a legend track as wide as the widest legend in it. They
follow `theme(legend.position = )`, so `"bottom"` puts them under each
panel (one track per row of panels, for
[`facet_grid()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/facet_wrap.md)
too) and `"inside"` inside each panel, and `legend.justification` aligns
them along the panel edge. Under each panel they take height from the
panels, so this example makes the plot taller; on a page where they
would leave the panels shorter than 25 mm, they are collected into the
plot’s legend instead, with a message.

``` r

vplot(mtcars, width = 8, height = 6) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(carb)) |>
  facet_grid(am ~ cyl, labeller = label_both) |>
  resolve_scale(color = "independent") |>
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

To collect them in the legend area instead, give the guide a position.
Each legend is then titled with the scale title and the panel’s strip
text:

``` r

vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(gear)) |>
  facet_wrap(~cyl, labeller = label_both) |>
  resolve_scale(color = "independent") |>
  guides(color = guide_legend(position = "right"))
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The guide position `"panel"` works for a shared scale too: its one
legend is repeated beside every panel.

Because colours are no longer comparable between panels, an independent
scale suits panels that are read one at a time. An unfaceted plot has a
single panel and ignores the setting.

## Composition

To place *different* plots side by side, build each one and combine
them.
[`concat()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/concat.md)
(and its friends
[`hconcat()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/concat.md)
and
[`vconcat()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/concat.md))
arrange plots into a grid; by default they collect the legends into one
shared guide.

``` r

p1 <- vplot(mtcars) |> mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))
p2 <- vplot(mtcars) |> mark_boxplot(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg)
p3 <- vplot(mtcars) |> mark_histogram(x = mpg, bins = 10)

concat(p1, p2, p3, ncol = 3, width = 9, height = 3.2)
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Each sub-plot brings its own size, so three 6-inch-wide plots in a row
make an 18-inch figure; pass `width` and `height` to size the whole
figure instead.
[`hconcat()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/concat.md)
takes `widths` and
[`vconcat()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/concat.md)
takes `heights` as well.

Control the shape with `ncol`/`nrow`, the relative sizes with
`widths`/`heights`, and irregular layouts with a `design` string.
[`plot_spacer()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/plot_spacer.md)
drops an empty cell, and
[`wrap_plots()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/concat.md)
takes a list of plots when you have assembled them programmatically.

``` r

concat(p1, p2, ncol = 1, heights = c(2, 1))
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Titles and tags

[`compose_annotation()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/compose_annotation.md)
adds text for the whole figure (`title`, `subtitle`, `caption`) and tags
each plot: `tag_levels = "A"` labels them A, B, C, and `"a"`, `"1"`,
`"i"` and `"I"` give the other styles. `tag_prefix` and `tag_suffix`
wrap each tag, as in `"(a)"` or `"A."`.

``` r

concat(p1, p2, p3, ncol = 3, width = 9, height = 3.2) |>
  compose_annotation(title = "Fuel economy", tag_levels = "A")
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Each row of plots gets a band above it as tall as its tallest tag, and
the tag sits in that band at the plot’s top-left corner, so it never
covers a title or a panel. The tags are drawn with the theme’s
`plot.tag` element, which sets their size, colour and `angle`; pass the
composition to
[`theme()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/theme_gray.md)
to change it. Titles and tags are drawn the same way in compositions
that can’t line up their panels (a faceted, polar, map or fixed-aspect
cell, a `design`, insets, a nested composition); spacers get no tag.
Legends are collected there too: every legend outside a panel moves to
the figure’s legend, identical ones drawn once, while a legend inside a
panel or beside each facet panel stays with its panel.

``` r

faceted <- vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  facet_wrap(~am, labeller = label_both)

concat(faceted, p3, ncol = 2, widths = c(2, 1), width = 8, height = 3.4) |>
  compose_annotation(
    title = "Weight, fuel economy and transmission",
    tag_levels = "a", tag_prefix = "(", tag_suffix = ")"
  )
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Every composition carries its own annotation, so a nested composition
can have a title and tags of its own:

``` r

inner <- concat(p1, p2, ncol = 2) |>
  compose_annotation(title = "By cylinders", tag_levels = "i")
concat(inner, p3, ncol = 1, width = 7, height = 6) |>
  compose_annotation(title = "Fuel economy", tag_levels = "A")
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A fixed-aspect plot
([`coord_fixed()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/coord_cartesian.md),
a theme `aspect.ratio`, a Venn diagram, a map) keeps its shape in a
composition: the figure gives it its own cell instead of stretching its
panel to line up with the others.

### Insets

[`inset()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/inset.md)
floats one plot over another, positioned by fractional coordinates of a
reference box. Good for an overview-plus-detail figure.

``` r

main <- vplot(mtcars) |> mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg)
mini <- vplot(mtcars) |> mark_histogram(x = mpg, bins = 8)
inset(main, mini, left = 0.5, bottom = 0.45, right = 1, top = 1)
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

`align_to` chooses the reference box, as patchwork’s `inset_element()`
does:

- `"panel"` (the default): the base plot’s panel area. In a faceted plot
  this spans all the panels, strips and gaps included.
- `"plot"`: the base plot without its title, subtitle and caption, with
  its axes and legends.
- `"full"`: the whole base cell, plot margin included.

The same fractions land in different places. Here the inset takes the
top-right quarter of the whole cell, title and margins included:

``` r

titled <- main |> labs(title = "Weight and fuel economy")
inset(titled, mini, left = 0.5, bottom = 0.5, right = 1, top = 1, align_to = "full")
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Before vellumplot 0.22.0 every inset was placed in the whole cell; pass
`align_to = "full"` to get that placement back. When the base is a
composition of several plots there is no single panel to align to, and
insets are placed in the whole figure.

### Sparklines

[`vsparkline()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/vsparkline.md)
is a compact, axis-free chart of a single series, sized in physical
units (mm by default) so it reads as a *word-sized graphic*. It is a
plain `PlotSpec` — render it, or
[`inset()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/inset.md) it
into a figure. Three shapes: a `"line"` trend (with a dot on its
extremes or last point), a `"bar"` column micro-chart, and a `"winloss"`
chart of equal up/down bars.

``` r

set.seed(1)
vsparkline(cumsum(rnorm(40)), width = 60, height = 16)
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

``` r

vsparkline(rpois(24, 6), type = "bar", color = "steelblue", width = 60, height = 16)
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Because it is a `PlotSpec`, a sparkline drops into any composition —
e.g. floated onto a plot as a tiny trend indicator:

``` r

spark <- vsparkline(cumsum(rnorm(40)))
inset(main, spark, left = 0.55, bottom = 0.8, right = 1, top = 1)
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Tables with sparklines

[`vtable()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/vtable.md)
lays a data frame out as a grid of cells: ordinary columns render as
text, and a **list-column of numeric vectors** renders as a per-row
sparkline. The whole table is one vector scene, so it prints and exports
like any plot — chart-in-table without leaving the plotting pipeline.

``` r

set.seed(1)
df <- data.frame(
  metric = c("Revenue", "Users", "Latency", "Errors"),
  latest = c(4213, 18402, 128, 37),
  change = c("+4.2%", "+1.1%", "-8ms", "-12%")
)
df$trend <- lapply(1:4, function(i) cumsum(rnorm(24)))
df$volume <- lapply(1:4, function(i) rpois(20, 6))

vtable(df, spark = list(trend = "line", volume = "bar"), row_height = 8)
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Map a column to a `type` (`"line"`/`"bar"`/`"winloss"`) or to a builder
function for full control,
e.g. `spark = list(trend = \(v) vsparkline(v, color = "steelblue"))`.

### Sparkline (and grob) callouts

`annotate("sparkline", …)` drops a sparkline at a data coordinate — a
little trend callout inside a plot. More generally,
`annotate("grob", grob = …)` places *any* vellum grob (or a `PlotSpec`)
at a coordinate, sized in physical units and anchored by
`halign`/`valign`.

``` r

set.seed(1)
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  annotate(
    "sparkline",
    x = 4, y = 33, values = cumsum(rnorm(30)),
    width = 32, height = 10, halign = "left"
  )
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Sparklines in a `gt` table

Beyond the native
[`vtable()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/vtable.md),
you can add a vellum sparkline column to a [gt](https://gt.rstudio.com)
table — keeping all of gt’s formatting and theming.
[`gt_vsparkline()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/gt_vsparkline.md)
renders a list-column of numeric vectors as inline-SVG sparklines (HTML
output).

``` r

library(gt)
set.seed(1)
df <- data.frame(metric = c("Revenue", "Users", "Latency", "Errors"))
df$trend <- lapply(1:4, function(i) cumsum(rnorm(24)))
df$volume <- lapply(1:4, function(i) rpois(20, 6))

gt(df) |>
  gt_vsparkline(trend, type = "line") |>
  gt_vsparkline(volume, type = "bar", color = "#4682b4")
```

| metric | trend | volume |
|----|----|----|
| Revenue | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Users | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Latency | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Errors | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |

Under the hood this uses
[`plot_svg()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/plot_svg.md),
which turns *any* vellumplot object into a self-contained SVG string —
so the same trick embeds a chart inline in `reactable` / `DT` cells or a
Quarto callout, not just gt. `inline = TRUE` drops the XML prolog so the
fragment goes straight into a paragraph, and
`recolor = c(grey30 = "currentColor")` makes the ink follow the
surrounding text colour (so it adapts to dark mode):

``` r

plot_svg(
  vsparkline(cumsum(rnorm(20)), color = "grey30"),
  inline = TRUE, recolor = c(grey30 = "currentColor")
)
```

### Repeat over a variable

[`repeat_()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/repeat_.md)
builds a small multiple by repeating one plot template across a set of
values, the composition-side counterpart to faceting when you want each
panel to be a fully independent plot rather than a shared-scale small
multiple.

Faceting and composition also compose with each other: a faceted plot is
still a spec, so it can go straight into a
[`concat()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/concat.md).
Once your figure looks right, send it to a file the same way as any
plot, with
[`render_plot()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/render_plot.md)
(see **[Get
started](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/articles/vellumplot.md)**).

## Multi-page and batch output

[`render_plot()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/render_plot.md)
writes one figure to one file. Two companions handle *many* figures at
once.

[`pdf_pages()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/pdf_pages.md)
writes a list of plots into a single PDF, one plot per page — a report
or a slide deck. Pages may differ in size (each plot keeps its own
`width`/`height`), and the per-page accessibility tags (see
**[Accessibility](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/articles/accessibility.md)**)
are written for every page.

``` r

report <- list(
  vplot(mtcars) |> mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |> labs(title = "Weight vs mpg"),
  vplot(mtcars) |> mark_histogram(x = mpg, bins = 10) |> labs(title = "mpg")
)
pdf_pages(report, "report.pdf")
```

Given a single *faceted* plot instead of a list,
[`pdf_pages()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/pdf_pages.md)
splits it into one page per facet cell — the paged counterpart of a
small-multiple grid, where each page trains its own scales and is tagged
independently:

``` r

vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  facet_wrap(~cyl) |>
  pdf_pages("by-cylinder.pdf")
```

For a slide deck you can edit,
[`vellum::pptx_pages()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellum/reference/pptx_pages.html)
takes the same kind of list and writes one PowerPoint slide per plot, as
editable shapes (see [Saving to
PowerPoint](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/articles/vellumplot.html#saving-to-powerpoint)):

``` r

vellum::pptx_pages(report, "report.pptx")
```

[`render_all()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/reference/render_all.md)
goes the other way: a list of plots to *separate* files, rendered across
CPU cores. Each plot is one independent job, so the work parallelises
cleanly (via process forks on macOS/Linux, sequentially on Windows) and
the output is byte-identical to rendering them one by one. When the list
is named, `paths` may be a single directory and each plot lands in
`<name>.png`:

``` r

render_all(
  list(
    weight = vplot(mtcars) |> mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg),
    power = vplot(mtcars) |> mark_point(x = hp, y = mpg)
  ),
  "figures/"
)
```
